## Learning goals

- **Choose** a review type that fits the purpose
- **Explain** what a review can and cannot establish
- **Translate** a topic into a concept table and a search string
- **Assess** a search: precision, recall, validation
- **Select** studies by explicit criteria; document in a **PRISMA** flow diagram
- **Synthesize** with a concept matrix
- **Identify** biases — in literature, databases, search and synthesis

::: {.notes}
- Choose: purpose decides the type, not the label
- Explain: limits as important as strengths
- Translate: topic → question → concept table → string
- Assess: how good is a search — recall, precision, test set
- Select: criteria fixed in advance · PRISMA: fate of every record
- Synthesise: by concept, not by author
- Identify: bias at every stage — name, reduce, report
:::

## How this lecture works

- **Aspired payoff:** the review section of your term paper or thesis gets better

- **Reference model:** the *systematic* literature review

- **Pause tasks:** stop the video, recap the chapters so far, then compare

- **Tutorial:** a separate step — after the video, on a search of your own

::: {.keybox .fragment}
A systematic review is the exception — but you always have a review section
:::

::: {.notes}
- Payoff: every term paper and thesis has a review section
- Reference model: systematic review — its standards improve any review
- Pause tasks: recap, answer from memory, then compare with the solution
- Tutorial: separate — real search, after the video
- Box: few write a stand-alone review · everyone writes a review section
:::

## One topic as a running example

::: {.dek}
Capabilities and routines — evolutionary economics meets business studies
:::

- **Routines:** the "genes" of the firm [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- **Absorptive capacity:** recognise, assimilate, apply external knowledge [@cohen1990absorptive]

- **Dynamic capabilities:** integrate, build, reconfigure competences [@teece1997dynamic]

- **Routine dynamics:** routines as a source of change [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
"How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure
capabilities and routines when explaining firm-level innovation?"
:::

::: {.notes}
- One literature through all chapters — evolutionary economics meets business studies
- Routines: Nelson & Winter — routines as the "genes" of firms
- Absorptive capacity: Cohen & Levinthal — learning needs prior knowledge
- Dynamic capabilities: Teece et al. — changing the resource base
- Routine dynamics: Feldman & Pentland — routines as a source of change
- Overlapping ideas, different words → ideal for every problem in this lecture
- Arrow: the question we come back to — made reviewable in ch. 2
:::

## What a review is for {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
01
:::

## A review is a study whose data are other studies

- **Map** a field — actors, concepts, methods

- **Establish** what is known, and how robustly

- **Find** gaps and contradictions

- **Build** or refine a framework

- **Justify** a research question

::: {.keybox .fragment}
No question → no review  · bad question → bad review
:::

::: {.notes}
- Review = study: question, method, checkable result
- Map: who works on what, with which concepts and methods
- Establish: what is known — and how robustly
- Find: gaps and contradictions — relative to the search
- Build: a framework from scattered work
- Justify: why your own question is worth asking
- Box: no question → just reading around
:::

## Review as a method ≠ review as a section

::: {.dek}
Same logic, different scale
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Stand-alone review: systematic
:::

- Review **is** the contribution

- Full protocol, several databases, at least two screeners

- Full **PRISMA** report

- e.g. @schilke2018quo
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Review section: non-systematic
:::

- Review **motivates** the contribution

- Optional: documented string, explicit criteria

- One **paragraph** + flow diagram, if anything

- Paper, thesis, report
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Learning the left is helpful for the right as well!
:::

::: {.notes}
- Left: stand-alone review — the review is the paper
  - full protocol, several databases, two screeners
  - full PRISMA report · example: Schilke et al. 2018
- Right: review section — motivates your own study
  - one database, documented string, explicit criteria
  - one paragraph + flow diagram — enough for a thesis
- Arrow: discipline of the left, at the scale of the right
:::

- Narrative / non-systematic: selective, interpretive · often undocumented ·
  not worthless, but not checkable

## Choose the review type by purpose

::: {.dek}
Purpose first, label second
:::

| Type | Purpose | Search | Synthesis | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:-------|:----------|:--------|
| Narrative | Overview, interpretation | Selective, often undocumented | Narrative | Textbook chapters |
| Systematic | Focused question | Exhaustive, reproducible | Structured, often thematic | @lane2006reification |
| Integrative | New framework from diverse work | Purposive, documented | Conceptual | @becker2004organizational |
| Scoping | Size and variety of a field | Broad, documented | Mapping, counts | @arksey2005scoping (method) |
| Meta-analysis | Pooled effect sizes | Exhaustive | Statistical | @orlitzky2003corporate |

: {.tasks .stepped}

::: {.source}
Simplified from @snyder2019literature and @grant2009typology. Lane et al.:
289 papers from 14 journals.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Purpose first, label second · real reviews mix types
- Narrative: overview, interpretation · search often undocumented · textbooks
- Systematic: focused question, exhaustive, reproducible · Lane et al.: 289
  papers, 14 journals
- Integrative: new framework from diverse work · Becker 2004 on routines
- Scoping: size and variety of a field
  - how much research, of what kind — not "does it work?"
  - often a pre-study for a systematic review · usually no quality appraisal
  - "mapping" = counting and categorising: years, disciplines, countries,
    methods, concepts
  - result: a map — where research is dense, where thin
- Meta-analysis: pooled effect sizes · Orlitzky et al. on CSR and financial
  performance
:::

## One literature, several review types

::: {.dek}
Capabilities: what each type delivers on the same subject
:::

- **Integrative:** routines literature "riddled with ambiguities"
  [@becker2004organizational]

- **Critical systematic:** absorptive capacity *reified* — widely used,
  rarely examined [@lane2006reification]

- **Content-analytic:** meta-framework of dynamic capabilities
  [@schilke2018quo]

- **Meta-analysis:** not meaningful — measures too different to pool

::: {.keybox .fragment}
State of the literature → possible review type
:::

::: {.notes}
- Same subject — what each type delivers
- Integrative: Becker — routines literature full of ambiguities
- Critical systematic: Lane et al. — absorptive capacity "reified": cited,
  not examined
- Content-analytic: Schilke et al. — meta-framework of dynamic capabilities
- Meta-analysis: not meaningful — measures too different to pool
- Box: state of the literature decides which type is possible
:::

## What a review can and cannot do

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review can
:::

- **Map** a debate and its positions

- **Establish** how much evidence exists, and of which kind

- **Show** agreement, conflict, context dependence

- **Locate** gaps — relative to a documented search

- **Clarify** inconsistently used concepts
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review cannot deliver
:::

- **Better evidence** than its primary studies

- **Proof of absence** — only "not found by this search"

- **Objectivity** through method — every step a choice

- **Causal answers** the primary studies lack

- **Evidence** from the frequency of a claim
:::
:::

::: {.keybox .fragment}
No substitute for reading the key works
:::

::: {.notes}
- Can:
  - Map: positions in a debate — who argues what
  - Establish: amount and kind of evidence
  - Show: where results agree, conflict, depend on context
  - Locate gaps: always relative to the documented search
  - Clarify: concepts used in different ways
- Cannot:
  - Better evidence: garbage in, garbage out
  - Proof of absence: only "not found by this search"
  - Objectivity: question, database, terms, criteria — all choices
  - Causal answers: not if the primary studies cannot give them
  - Frequency: often claimed ≠ well supported
- Box: no substitute for reading the key works
- Naming limits = competence, not weakness
:::

## Spotlight: QWERTY — mapped, not settled

::: {.dek}
Path dependence · contested for decades
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Lock-in
:::

- Technical interrelatedness, scale economies, quasi-irreversibility
  [@david1985clio]

::: {.fragment .consequence}
→ markets can lock in **inferior** standards
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
"Fable of the keys"
:::

- Weak evidence for Dvorak's superiority, partly from Dvorak himself
  [@liebowitz1990fable]

::: {.fragment .consequence}
→ lock-in claim **not established**
:::
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Review: which evidence each side rests on
:::

::: {.notes}
- Path dependence — classic example, contested for decades
- Left, David 1985: interrelatedness, scale economies, quasi-irreversibility
  - → markets can lock in an inferior standard
- Right, Liebowitz & Margolis 1990: evidence for Dvorak weak, partly from
  Dvorak himself
  - → lock-in claim not established
- Arrow: review maps which evidence each side rests on — does not settle it
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 1 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
Claim: "My systematic review shows there is no research on dynamic
capabilities in family firms."

- Why might the claim be wrong? Two reasons
- Rewrite it so that it claims only what the search shows
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[Solution]{.solhead}

- **Only this search:** "not found" means not found *in this database with
  this string* — coverage, missing abstracts, language
- **Other words:** "family business", "family-owned" · capabilities also as
  "routines", "absorptive capacity" — a narrow string misses them
- **Rewording:** "Our search (OpenAlex, titles and abstracts, date, string in
  appendix) found no empirical study that …"
:::

::: {.notes}
- Goal: apply "a review cannot prove absence"
- Claim sounds like a finding — it is a statement about a search
- Reason 1: one database, one string — coverage, missing abstracts, language
- Reason 2: other words — family business; routines, absorptive capacity
- Rewording: what was searched, what was not found
- Reader judges how far that goes
:::

## Workflow and question {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
02
:::

## Six stages

::: {.dek}
Each stage constrains the next · question changed after the results ≈ p-hacking
:::

::: {.stages}
1. **Protocol:** question, scope, criteria **written down**

2. **Search:** documented and rerunnable

3. **Screening:** criteria applied to titles, abstracts, full texts

4. **Extraction:** the same fixed format for every study

5. **Synthesis:** by concept, not by author — explain agreement and disagreement

6. **Reporting:** what you did, what you found, what your choices cost
:::

::: {.source}
After @tranfield2003towards: the medical template adapted to management
research.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Each stage constrains the next
- Question changed after seeing results ≈ p-hacking
- Protocol: written down before any search
- Search: documented, so that someone else can rerun it
- Screening: criteria only — titles and abstracts, then full texts
- Extraction: same format for every study
- Synthesis: by concept · explain agreement and disagreement
- Reporting: including what your choices cost
- Top right from now on: which stage we are in
- Source: Tranfield et al. — medical template adapted to management
:::

## A topic is not a question {data-stage="1"}

::: {.continuum}
<div class="cline"></div>

::: {.cpos .left}
[Too broad]{.chead}

"What do we know about capabilities?"

Thousands of hits · no criteria possible
:::

::: {.cpos .right .fragment}
[Too narrow]{.chead}

"Does absorptive capacity raise patenting in German biotech SMEs in 2015?"

A handful of studies · nothing to synthesise
:::

::: {.cpos .mid .fragment}
[Reviewable]{.chead}

"How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure capabilities and routines
when explaining firm-level innovation?"

Object · context · what you want to know
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Scope of a question: a line between two extremes
- Too broad: a whole field · thousands of hits · no criteria possible
- Too narrow: a handful of studies · nothing to compare
- Reviewable: in between — object, context, what you want to know
- Test: two people, same in/out decisions?
:::

## Two frameworks for a reviewable question {data-stage="1"}

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
PCC: *what is known about X?*
:::

- **P**opulation: firms

- **C**oncept: capabilities and routines — defined and measured how?

- **C**ontext: empirical innovation research

::: {.fragment}
*Lecture: the running example*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
PICO: *does X affect Y?*
:::

- **P**opulation: employees, firms

- **I**ntervention: working time reduction

- **C**omparison: regular working hours

- **O**utcome: productivity, well-being

::: {.fragment}
*Tutorial: the four-day week*
:::
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Elements → criteria · usually only I and O (or the concept) → search string
:::

::: {.source}
PCC = Population, Concept, Context — @peters2015guidance, for scoping
reviews. PICO = Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome —
@richardson1995wellbuilt, from clinical medicine.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Checklists from the health sciences — nothing missing from the question
- PCC: what is known about X? — scoping questions
  - Population: firms
  - Concept: capabilities and routines — defined, measured how?
  - Context: empirical innovation research
  - → the lecture's running example
- PICO: does X affect Y? — effects questions, needs a comparison
  - Population: employees, firms
  - Intervention: in management often a practice or institution
  - Comparison: regular working hours
  - Outcome: productivity, well-being
  - → the tutorial's example
- Arrow: P and C → inclusion criteria · I and O, or the concept → string
:::

## The concept table: building blocks of the search {data-stage="1"}

::: {.dek}
One column per concept · one row per wording
:::

| Capabilities & routines | Innovation | Empirical measurement |
|:------------------------|:-----------|:----------------------|
| dynamic capabilities | innovation, innovative | measurement, measure |
| organizational / organisational routines | "new product" | operationalization / operationalisation |
| absorptive capacity | patent | empirical |
| organizational / organisational capabilities | R&D | survey |
| technological capabilities | | "panel data" |
| competences, competencies | | |

: {.lg}

::: {.source}
Spelling variants listed explicitly · plural forms covered by stemming ·
third column: in the string or in the criteria — document the choice
:::

::: {.notes}
- One column per concept, one row per wording
- Column 1: capabilities and routines — many communities, many words
- Column 2: innovation — incl. proxies: patent, R&D, new product
- Column 3: empirical measurement — kind of study, not its subject
  - option A: third AND block in the string → fewer hits, loses studies
    whose abstract does not say "empirical"
  - option B: screening criterion "empirical only" → more to screen, no
    losses from wording
  - both legitimate — decide, write it down
- Source line: spelling variants listed · plurals via stemming
:::

## Criteria for inclusion: fixed before the results {data-stage="1"}

::: {.dek}
Part of the protocol · replicable by a second person
:::

- **Content:** capability or routine construct, related to innovation

- **Design:** empirical, quantitative or qualitative; conceptual papers out

- **Type:** peer-reviewed articles, reviews; book chapters out — with reason

- **Period, language:** e.g. 1990 onwards, English → **reported limitation**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Contestable is fine — invisible is not
:::

::: {.notes}
- Fixed before seeing results — part of the protocol
- Content: capability or routine construct, related to innovation
- Design: empirical, quantitative or qualitative · conceptual papers out
- Type: articles, reviews · book chapters out — give the reason
- Period, language: e.g. 1990 onwards, English → report as a limitation
- Box: criteria may be contested — but must be visible
:::

## Searching {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
03
:::

## Not every search system fits a systematic review {data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
Requirements: reliable search · precise query · documented, rerunnable
:::

- **OpenAlex:** free, open, broad coverage, Boolean, scriptable
  [@priem2022openalex]

- **EconBiz:** free subject portal for economics — books, working papers,
  German [@zbw2026econbiz]

- **Web of Science, Scopus:** curated, precise syntax — paid, access fragile

- **Google Scholar:** huge coverage — limited Boolean control, ranked, not
  reproducible

- Many systems not fit for systematic reviews [@gusenbauer2020which]

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Baseline: OpenAlex · economics: + EconBiz · paid databases: optional, with benefits
:::

::: {.notes}
- Requirements: reliable search · precise query · rerunnable
- OpenAlex: free, open, same for everyone — baseline of this lecture
- EconBiz: ZBW portal — books, working papers, German
  - searches abstracts, does not show them · no citations
- Web of Science, Scopus: precise syntax, curated — paid, access ends with
  graduation
- Google Scholar: fine for a paper you know — not for the search of a review
- Gusenbauer & Haddaway: many systems fail these requirements
- Box: OpenAlex baseline · EconBiz for economics · paid databases optional
:::

## Three families of search tools {data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
Different logics → different roles in a review
:::

::: {.grid3}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[Keyword (Boolean) search]{.caphead}

Matches your terms · transparent, reproducible · blind to unknown words
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Semantic (AI) search]{.caphead}

Matches meaning · reveals vocabulary · opaque, not reproducible
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Citation-based search]{.caphead}

**Snowballing** from seed papers · finds what keywords miss — within one
community
:::
:::

::: {.cap .centred .fragment}
[In a review]{.caphead}

Boolean: **backbone** · semantic: **input** to the concept table · citation:
**supplement**
:::

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Non-systematic additions are fine **if documented** — e.g. expert suggestions
:::

::: {.notes}
- Different logics → different roles
- Keyword: matches your terms — transparent, blind to words you don't know
- Semantic: matches meaning — reveals vocabulary · opaque, not rerunnable
- Citation: snowballing — follows links from seed papers · finds what
  keywords miss, within one community
- In a review: Boolean backbone · semantic input · citation supplement
- Box: expert tips, chance finds — fine · own count in the flow diagram,
  same criteria
:::

## From concept table to search string {data-stage="2"}

::: {.code-lg}
```text
("dynamic capabilities" OR "organizational routines" OR "organisational routines"
 OR "absorptive capacity" OR "organizational capabilities"
 OR "organisational capabilities" OR "technological capabilities")
AND (innovation OR innovative OR "new product" OR patent)
AND (measurement OR measure OR empirical OR survey)
```
:::

- **Operators:** AND, OR, NOT — in capitals · OR within a concept, AND between

- **Quotation marks:** phrases

- **Stemming:** always on — "routines" finds "routine"; spellings and
  derivations listed

- **Filters:** years, type, language — documented separately

::: {.source}
OpenAlex syntax, field `title_and_abstract.search`; stemming off only with
`.search.exact`. No wildcards in the web interface. Current rules: OpenAlex
help pages and tutorial.
:::

::: {.notes}
- String = concept table written out
- Operators: in capitals · OR within a concept, AND between concepts
- Quotation marks: exact phrase
- Stemming:
  - word reduced to its stem — in records and query
  - "routine" = "routines": identical counts (6 Nov 2026)
  - always on, nothing in the string activates it · off only via
    `.search.exact` (API)
  - no thesaurus: spelling variants, derived forms → list them
- Filters: separate from the string — document them
- No wildcards in the web interface
:::

## Every search trades recall against precision {data-stage="2"}

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Recall (sensitivity)
:::

- Share of all **relevant** papers found

- Low → review **incomplete**, unnoticed
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Precision
:::

- Share of **found** papers that are relevant

- Low → **thousands** of irrelevant titles to screen
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Wider string: recall ↑ precision ↓ · narrower: the reverse
:::

::: {.notes}
- Recall: share of all relevant papers found — denominator unknown
- Low recall → review incomplete, nobody notices
- Precision: share of found papers that are relevant
- Low precision → thousands of titles to screen
- Arrow: trade-off — wider string: recall up, precision down
:::

## Recall: tested against known papers {data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
All relevant papers: unknown · some: known · missed known → missed unknown
:::

- Before searching: **key papers** that must appear — 5–10 in a review, 3–5 for a term paper

- Incl. **closed-access** papers from large publishers (next slide)

- Run the string → how many retrieved?

- **Missed one?** Its title and keywords → the missing term

- Revise, rerun, **log every version**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Illustrative: v1 finds 5/8 → + "competenc\*", "routine\*" → v2 finds 8/8
:::

::: {.notes}
- All relevant papers unknown → known ones as a sample
- Key papers chosen before searching — 5–10 in a review, 3–5 in a term paper
- Include closed-access papers → abstract gap visible (next slide)
- Run the string → how many found?
- Missed one → its title and keywords → the missing term
- Every version into the search log
- Box: illustrative — v1 5/8, terms added, v2 8/8
:::

## The blind spot: records without abstract {data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
No abstract → title and keywords only · gap not random
:::

- ~**40%** of OpenAlex records without abstract [@borrego2025openalex]

- Concentrated: **closed-access** Elsevier and Springer Nature articles — core
  outlets in business and economics [@kramer2024open]

- Consequence: **recall loss** for exactly these papers

- Adding abstracts later: helps **screening**, not **search**

::: {.notes}
- No abstract → only title and keywords can match
- ~40% of OpenAlex records without abstract — Borrego et al.
- Concentrated: closed-access Elsevier, Springer Nature — core outlets in
  business and economics
- → recall loss exactly there
- Abstract on the publisher page helps screening — only for records found
- Why it happens → ch. 6
:::

## Countermeasures: what the method can compensate {data-stage="2"}

- **Snowballing:** citation links independent of abstracts

- **Test set** with closed-access papers → gap visible

- **Title terms:** words authors put in titles

- **Measure** the gap: share of hits without abstract, by publisher and year

- **Report** it as a limitation

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Optional add-on: same string in a paid database — compare hit lists
:::

::: {.notes}
- Snowballing: citation links need no abstracts → compulsory
- Test set with closed-access papers: found? if not → abstracts cost recall
- Title terms: labels authors put in titles ("dynamic capabilities") — not
  abstract words ("empirical")
- Measure: share without abstract, by publisher and year
- Report: that number goes into the limitations
- Box: paid database as a comparison — optional
:::

## Spotlight: words follow communities {data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
Capabilities: overlapping ideas, different names
:::

- **Evolutionary economics:** routines, organisational capabilities
  [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- **Strategic management:** dynamic capabilities, resources, core competences
  [@teece1997dynamic]

- **Organisation studies:** routine dynamics [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

- **Innovation and development studies:** technological capabilities,
  absorptive capacity [@cohen1990absorptive]

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Use only "dynamic capabilit\*" → present one community's view as "the field"
:::

::: {.notes}
- Same phenomenon, community-specific names
- Evolutionary economics: routines, organisational capabilities
- Strategic management: dynamic capabilities, resources, core competences
- Organisation studies: routine dynamics
- Innovation and development studies: technological capabilities,
  absorptive capacity
- Arrow: one community's term → its view sold as "the field"
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 3 {.no-dash data-stage="2"}

::: {.dek}
Applies: recall and precision
:::

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
4,800 records · all 8 test papers found

- What does this say about recall and precision?
- Your options?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[Solution]{.solhead}

- **Recall:** probably high — but tested only on papers you already knew
- **Precision:** probably low — thousands of titles to screen
- **Options:** sharper terms, another AND block, filters — each documented;
  after every change, the test set must still be found · or estimate
  precision on a random sample of 50 and screen everything
:::

::: {.notes}
- Goal: recall vs. precision
- 8/8 test papers → recall probably high — but only on known papers
- 4,800 records → precision probably low
- Options: sharper terms, extra AND block, filters — retest each time
- Or estimate precision on a sample of 50, then screen everything
:::

## Pause: recap chapters 1–3 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
Stop the video — answer from memory:

- Three review types — and the purpose of each?
- What makes a question reviewable?
- Recall vs. precision — and how a test set checks recall?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[Solution]{.solhead}

- **Types:** narrative — overview · scoping — map a field · systematic —
  focused question, reproducible · meta-analysis — pooled effects
- **Reviewable:** object · context · what you want to know (PICO, PCC) —
  two people, same in/out decisions
- **Recall:** relevant papers found · **precision:** found papers relevant ·
  test set: known papers that must appear
:::

::: {.notes}
- Stop the video, answer from memory — then the solution
- Types: ch. 1 · reviewable question: ch. 2
- Recall, precision, test set: ch. 3
- Snowballing: compensates missing abstracts

## Screening and selection {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
04
:::

## Screening in two rounds {data-stage="3"}

::: {.dek}
Cheap decisions first · protocol criteria only
:::

- **Round 1 — titles, abstracts:** clearly out → exclude; in doubt → keep

- **No abstract?** Publisher page via DOI — abstracts free to read there

- **Round 2 — full texts:** decide; **reason** for every exclusion

- **Second screener:** all records, or a sample; disagreements resolved; compmute interrater agreement

- **Criteria drift:** criterion changed → restart, document

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
One row per record + reason column → template in the tutorial
:::

::: {.notes}
- Cheap decisions first · protocol criteria only
- Round 1: titles, abstracts — clearly out → exclude · in doubt → keep
- No abstract: publisher page via DOI — free to read
- Round 2: full texts — a reason for every exclusion
- Second screener: all records or a sample · resolve disagreements
- Criteria drift: criterion changed → re-screen, document
- Arrow: one row per record — template in the tutorial
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 4 {.no-dash data-stage="3"}

::: {.dek}
Applies: screening and documenting decisions
:::

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
- Reasons for every full-text exclusion — but not for title/abstract
  exclusions: why?
- What can a reader do with the documented reasons?
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[Solution]{.solhead}

- **Why:** title/abstract exclusions are many and mostly obvious — reasons
  would cost much and say little; full-text exclusions are the close calls
- **Reader:** check that criteria were applied consistently · judge whether
  excluded studies could change the conclusion · disagree with a decision,
  visibly
:::

::: {.notes}
- Goal: where reasons are needed, and why
- Title/abstract: many, mostly obvious exclusions — reasons cost much, say
  little
- Full text: close calls → reasons make the judgement checkable
- Reader: check consistency · judge impact on conclusions · disagree visibly
:::

05

## Weak reviews: a list of summaries {data-stage="5"}

::: {.dek}
Same sources · organised by author vs. by idea
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Author-centric
:::

- "Nelson and Winter (1982) describe … Teece et al. (1997) define …
  Feldman and Pentland (2003) argue …"

- Reader: **so what?**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Concept-centric
:::

- "The literature disagrees on whether routines stabilise or change firms …"

- Stability (Nelson & Winter) vs. change from within (Feldman & Pentland)

- The disagreement **is** the finding
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Same sources, two ways of organising
- Left: author by author — each sentence a summary
- Reader left with "so what?"
- Right: starts from the debate — do routines stabilise or change firms?
- Sources as evidence for positions
- Disagreement is the finding · dynamic capabilities as an attempted bridge
:::

## Spotlight: firm growth — sorting conflicting results {data-stage="5"}

::: {.dek}
Gibrat's law: growth independent of size · concept matrix, illustrative rows
:::

| Study | Sample | Size classes | Result |
|:------|:-------|:-------------|:-------|
| A | All firms, incl. exits | All | Small firms grow faster → law **rejected** |
| B | Survivors only | All | Small firms grow faster → law **rejected** |
| C | Survivors only | Above minimum size | No size effect → law **holds** |
| D | Survivors only | Above minimum size | No size effect → law **holds** |

: {.lg .stepped}

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Vote count 2 : 2 → nothing · sorted by sample → **when** the law holds
:::

::: {.source}
Pattern after @mansfield1962entry and @santarelli2006gibrat; book-length
synthesis: @coad2009growth.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Gibrat's law: growth independent of size
- Rows illustrative · pattern from the literature
- A: all firms incl. exits → small firms grow faster → rejected
- B: survivors, all sizes → rejected
- C, D: above minimum size → law holds
- Arrow: vote count says nothing · column "sample" says when it holds
- Surveys add sector, country, period
:::

## Quality appraisal: not all studies count the same {data-stage="4 5"}

::: {.dek}
Record it in the matrix · use it in the text
:::

- **Construct:** clearly defined, consistently measured?

- **Design:** able to support the claim?

- **Sample:** described — who is missing?

- **Limitations:** acknowledged by the authors?

::: {.keybox .fragment}
In your text: strong evidence first, weak evidence qualified — never silently
dropped
:::

::: {.notes}
- Not exclusion — weighting
- Construct: clearly defined, consistently measured?
- Design: can it support the claim, e.g. a causal one?
- Sample: described — who is missing?
- Limitations: named by the authors?
- Answers → quality column of the matrix
- Box: "two panel studies find …; three cross-sectional surveys suggest …"
- Check: conclusion without the weakest studies?
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 5 {.no-dash data-stage="5"}

::: {.dek}
Applies: from summary to synthesis
:::

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
The review section of a paper you recently read:

- Author- or concept-centric?
- Sketch the concept matrix it should have used
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[What to look for]{.solhead}

- **Author-centric:** paragraphs start with names — "X (2010) shows …"
- **Concept-centric:** paragraphs start with a claim or a debate; sources
  as evidence
- **Matrix:** rows = cited studies · columns = what the paper's question
  needs — construct, design, context, finding
:::

::: {.notes}
- Goal: recognise synthesis vs. summary
- Author-centric: names open the paragraphs
- Concept-centric: claims open the paragraphs
- Matrix: rows = cited studies · columns = what the question needs
:::

## Biases, limitations, caveats {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
06
:::

## Bias at every stage

::: {.dek}
Inherited from the literature → report · introduced by you → reduce
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[The literature]{.caphead}

Publication bias · citation bias · survivorship in primary samples
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Database and search]{.caphead}

Coverage bias · terminology bias · ranking and tool effects
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Screening]{.caphead}

Confirmation bias · single-screener judgement · criteria drift
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Synthesis and reporting]{.caphead}

Vote counting · apples and oranges · overclaiming from absence
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Two kinds: inherited → report · introduced by you → reduce
- Literature: publication, citation, survivorship
- Database and search: coverage, terminology, ranking
- Screening: confirmation bias, single screener, criteria drift
- Synthesis: vote counting, apples and oranges, overclaiming from absence
:::

## Publication bias: a filtered literature {data-bias="1"}

- Significant, novel, positive → more likely published

- Counting published results → measuring the publication process, too

- **Economics overall:** 159 literatures — ~**80%** of effects exaggerated,
  typically **× 2** [@ioannidis2017power]

- **Corporate Social Responsability and profitability:**
  - 2003, 52 studies: clearly **positive** link [@orlitzky2003corporate]
  - 2023, 512 studies, corrected for publication bias: **small**
    [@hirsch2023csr]

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Same question, more studies, bias corrected → a much weaker answer
:::

::: {.notes}
- Significant, new, positive → published more often, faster
- Counting published results = also counting what journals accept
- Economics: 159 literatures · ~4 of 5 effects exaggerated, typically ×2 —
  Ioannidis et al.
- CSR and profitability:
  - Orlitzky et al. 2003, 52 studies: clearly positive
  - Hirsch et al. 2023, 512 studies, corrected for bias: small
- Arrow: more studies, bias corrected → much weaker answer
:::

## Citation bias: often cited ≠ well supported {data-bias="1"}

::: {.dek}
Citations attract citations · works cited for what they are believed to say
:::

- Absorptive capacity, 289 papers: construct **reified** — used as given,
  rarely examined [@lane2006reification]

- Citation-based tools: **amplify** — they find what is already cited

- AI summaries: **amplify** again — the dominant reading

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Read the original · check how it is used
:::

::: {.notes}
- Citations attract citations · cited for what they are believed to say
- Lane et al.: absorptive capacity reified — 289 papers, used as given
- Citation-based tools find what is already cited → amplify
- AI summaries reproduce the dominant reading → amplify again
- Box: read the original · check how it is used
:::

## Survivorship bias: inherited from primary studies {data-bias="1"}

::: {.dek}
Aggregation can hide it
:::

- Survivors-only growth samples: exited small firms missing → small firms
  look faster-growing (cf. @mansfield1962entry)

- Capability building: failed attempts rarely observed

- **Record** each study's sample design in the matrix — survivors only, or
  incl. exits? — or the bias is averaged in

::: {.notes}
- Inherited from the primary studies · hidden by aggregation
- Survivors-only growth samples: exited small firms missing → small firms
  look faster-growing
- Capability building: failed attempts rarely observed
- Remedy: sample design as a matrix column → compare, don't average (firm
  growth slide)
:::

## Coverage bias: the database decides {data-bias="2"}

::: {.dek}
Curation = selection · selection ≠ neutral
:::

- Web of Science, Scopus: natural sciences and **English** over-, **social
  sciences** and humanities under-represented [@mongeon2016journal]

- **Books, working papers, Global South:** weak in curated databases

- OpenAlex: broader, less English-centred — but **metadata gaps**: abstracts,
  language tags [@cespedes2025linguistic]

- Subject portals (EconBiz): books, **German** — but one discipline only
  [@zbw2026econbiz]

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
No neutral database · test with known papers, report the gaps
:::

::: {.notes}
- Curation = selection · selection ≠ neutral
- Web of Science, Scopus: natural sciences, English over · social sciences,
  humanities under — Mongeon & Paul-Hus
- Books, working papers, Global South: weak in curated databases
- OpenAlex: broader, less English-centred — gaps in abstracts, language tags
- EconBiz: books, German — one discipline only
- Arrow: no neutral database → test with known papers, report the gaps
:::

## Terminology bias: the pluralism problem of search {data-bias="2"}

::: {.dek}
Search terms encode a perspective
:::

- "Dynamic capabilities" ≠ "routines" ≠ "technological capabilities" — yet
  overlapping

- Heterodox vs. mainstream: different **names**, same phenomenon

- Result: **systematic**, yet **one-sided**


::: {.keybox .fragment}
**Countermeasures:** terms from several communities, alternative strings,
  compared hit lists
:::


::: {.notes}
- Search terms encode a perspective
- Dynamic capabilities, routines, technological capabilities — overlapping,
  not identical
- Heterodox vs. mainstream: different names, same phenomenon
- Result: systematic, yet one-sided
- Countermeasures: terms from several communities · alternative strings ·
  compare hit lists
:::

## Political economy: who owns the record of science? {data-bias="2"}

::: {.dek}
What you can find depends on who controls publications and metadata
:::

- Five publishers in Web of Science: **33%** of papers in 1980 → **59%** in
  2021 — fewer in broader indexes [@lariviere2015oligopoly;
  @vanbellen2025hidden]

- Owners of the indexes: **Elsevier** → Scopus · **Clarivate** → Web of Science

- Abstracts withdrawn from open indexes: Springer Nature 2022, Elsevier 2024

  — Abstracts as **assets**, e.g. for AI licensing [@kramer2024open]

- Counter-movement: **open research information** — Barcelona Declaration
  2024; Sorbonne and CNRS leave commercial databases [@barcelona2024declaration]

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Missing abstracts: a political decision, not a technical accident
:::

::: {.notes}
- Who controls publications and metadata decides what you find
- Web of Science: big five 33% (1980) → 59% (2021) · Dimensions: 44% (2021)
  — concentration depends on the index
- Scopus = Elsevier · Web of Science = Clarivate — indexes are products
- Abstracts withdrawn: Springer Nature 2022, Elsevier 2024 — readable on
  publisher pages, not redistributable
- Abstracts as assets — e.g. AI licensing
- Counter-movement: Barcelona Declaration 2024 · Sorbonne → OpenAlex 2024 ·
  CNRS left Scopus 2024, Web of Science 2026
- Arrow: choosing a database = choosing an infrastructure
:::

## Reviewer bias: screening and synthesis {data-bias="3 4"}

::: {.dek}
Reviewer = part of the instrument · protocol = constraint
:::

- **Confirmation bias:** fitting borderline papers stay in

- **Criteria drift:** criteria change while reading

- **Vote counting:** significant results counted, evidence not weighed

- **Apples and oranges:** different constructs and designs pooled

- **Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Fixed criteria · second screener · concept matrix · careful wording
:::

::: {.notes}
- About you — the reviewer as part of the instrument
- Confirmation bias: borderline papers that fit stay in
- Criteria drift: early and late records judged differently
- Vote counting: counting significance instead of weighing evidence
- Apples and oranges: pooling different constructs and designs
- Absence of evidence: "no study found" ≠ "no effect"
- Box: countermeasures already known — criteria, second screener, matrix,
  wording
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 6 {.no-dash data-bias="1 4"}

::: {.dek}
Applies: biases in the literature and in the synthesis
:::

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
40 studies on dynamic capabilities and performance · 32 significantly positive

- Why not conclude: "works in 80% of firms"?
- Give three reasons for your assessment
:::

::: {.answer .fragment .nonincremental}
[Solution]{.solhead}

- **Publication bias:** null and negative results less often published —
  the 8 may be the visible tip
- **Vote counting:** significance ≠ size · 80% of *studies*, not of
  *firms*
- **Apples and oranges, survivors:** different measures and samples;
  failed firms rarely observed
:::

::: {.notes}
- Goal: biases in literature and synthesis
- 32 of 40 positive — sounds strong
- Publication bias: the null results may be missing
- Vote counting: share of studies ≠ share of firms · significance ≠ size
- Apples and oranges, survivorship: different measures, failed firms unseen
:::

- What does a flow diagram show?

- **Screening:** round 1 titles and abstracts, in doubt keep · round 2 full

- **Synthesis:** organised by ideas, not authors · matrix read by column →
  agreement, disagreement, conditions
- **Bias:** inherited — publication, citation, survivorship · yours —
  confirmation bias, criteria drift, vote counting
:::

- Biases: ch. 6

07
:::

## Reproducible from the report alone {data-stage="6"}

- **Database** and date of the search

- **Full string**, all filters — or the query URL / script

- **Criteria**, and who screened

- **Numbers** per stage → flow diagram

- **Synthesis** method — and the **limitations** of all the above

::: {.source}
@page2021prisma; @rethlefsen2021prismas. Search log template → tutorial.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Test: could someone rerun the search from the report?
- Database and date
- Full string and filters — or query URL, script
- Criteria, and who screened
- Numbers per stage → flow diagram
- Synthesis method — and the limitations
- PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S · search log template in the tutorial
:::

## Limitations: as specific as the method {data-stage="6"}

::: {.dek}
The bias · its direction · why accepted
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Generic
:::

- "Some relevant studies may have been missed."
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Specific
:::

- OpenAlex, titles and abstracts; 41 of 411 hits without abstract, mostly
  Elsevier and Springer Nature (tutorial example)

::: {.fragment .consequence}
→ recall loss for closed-access articles: one test paper found by no route
:::

::: {.fragment .consequence}
→ snowballing added 13 studies; residual gap reported
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Formula: the bias · its direction · why accepted
- Generic: true of every review — says nothing
- Specific: the tutorial's example review — 41 of 411 hits without abstract,
  mostly Elsevier and Springer Nature
- Direction: recall loss for closed-access articles · a 1973 test paper
  found neither by the string nor by snowballing
- Response: snowballing added 13 studies · residual gap reported
:::

## AI: helpful at some stages, risky at others

::: {.dek}
AI suggests · the documented, reproducible step is yours
:::

| Stage | AI can help with | Typical failure | Rule |
|:------|:-----------------|:----------------|:-----|
| Question, concept table | Synonyms, neighbouring vocabularies | Converges on dominant terms | Check terms against key papers |
| Search | Papers you missed | Opaque, non-reproducible | Never the primary search |
| Screening | First sort of titles | Plausible but wrong exclusions | You decide; log reasons |
| Extraction | Reading many PDFs | Silent errors across the sample | Verify a sample by hand |
| Synthesis, writing | Structure, critique of drafts | Generic, mainstream synthesis | Your matrix, your argument |

: {.lg .stepped tbl-colwidths="[19,27,27,27]"}

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Disclose every use
:::

::: {.notes}
- AI suggests · the documented, reproducible step is yours
- Question: synonyms — converges on dominant terms → check against key papers
- Search: may find missed papers — opaque → never the primary search
- Screening: first sort — plausible wrong exclusions → you decide, log reasons
- Extraction: many PDFs — silent errors → verify a sample by hand
- Synthesis: structure, critique — generic, mainstream → your matrix, your
  argument
- Arrow: disclose every use
:::

- **Missing anything?** Then the search cannot be rerun — only retold

::: {.notes}

- Search: database, route, date, string, field, filters, URL or script
- Selection: criteria, screeners, numbers
- Anything missing → the search can only be retold, not rerun

## Wrap-up {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

08

## What to take away

- A review = a **study**: question, method, checkable result

- **Open baseline:** concept table → OpenAlex string → test → snowball → log

- **Synthesis** by concept — via the concept matrix

- Bias at **every** stage, incl. database ownership: reduce, then report

- AI **suggests** — the documented step is **yours**

::: {.keybox .lg .fragment}
Systematic ≠ objective — choices made visible
:::

::: {.notes}
- Review = study: question, method, checkable result
- Open baseline: concept table → OpenAlex → test → snowball → log
- Synthesis by concept, via the matrix
- Bias everywhere — incl. who owns the databases
- AI suggests · you decide and document
- Box: systematic ≠ objective — choices made visible
:::

## Can and cannot, once more

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review can
:::

- Map a debate — QWERTY, routines, Gibrat

- Show context dependence

- Locate gaps relative to a documented search
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review cannot
:::

- Exceed its primary studies

- Prove absence

- Turn frequency into evidence
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Can: map a debate — QWERTY, routines, Gibrat
- Can: show context dependence — e.g. firm size and growth
- Can: locate gaps — relative to the search
- Cannot: exceed its primary studies
- Cannot: prove absence
- Cannot: turn frequency into evidence
:::
